 9                THE SECRETARY:   Legislative 

10   Resolution 4687, by Senator Murphy, 

11   memorializing Governor Andrew M. Cuomo to 

12   proclaim April 2016 as Distracted Driving Month 

13   in the State of New York.

14                ACTING PRESIDENT GRIFFO:   Senator 

15   Murphy.

16                SENATOR MURPHY:   Thank you, 

17   Mr. President.

18                This resolution sheds light on an 

19   important issue that we see each and every day 

20   as we drive around:  Distracted driving.  April 

21   is Distracted Driving Month.  

22                And distracted driving isn't just 

23   something that we shrug our shoulders at, 

24   because it has proven to take lives.  And one 

25   such life that was taken from us was Evan 


                                                                1900

 1   Lieberman.  In 2011, Evan was killed in a head-on 

 2   car accident.  The driver of the other car was on 

 3   their cellphone.

 4                Now, while I did not have the honor 

 5   of meeting Evan, I did have the great privilege 

 6   of getting to know his family.  I remember 

 7   meeting Mr. Lieberman in my office, and he told 

 8   me about the tragic and avoidable death of his 

 9   young son.  

10                While Mr. Lieberman and his entire 

11   family will miss his son, they have turned a true 

12   tragedy into a positive mission of bringing 

13   awareness to distracted driving.

14                The facts are staggering.  In 2014, 

15   we've had over 3,000 people die of distracted 

16   driving, more than 400 people injured due to 

17   distracted driving.  

18                The cellphones, the texting -- I see 

19   a lot of young kids here today, please be careful 

20   in the cars -- turning on the radio.  It has 

21   become a major problem.  And as a father myself 

22   of three kids, I am teaching my kids about this 

23   distracted driving, and we are shedding light on 

24   this serious issue.

25                I would just like to acknowledge 


                                                                1901

 1   Mr. Lieberman -- I believe he is here today -- 

 2   and thank him and allow him the privilege of 

 3   being in Senate chambers and keeping awareness to 

 4   this very, very important issue.

 6   Supervisor Rob Greenstein, who's here today, who 

 7   has taken initiative himself within his town on 

 8   having magnets:  "Hands off the phone and on the 

 9   wheel.  Please pay attention."  

10                Mr. President, I thank you for the 

11   honor and courtesy.

13   you, Senator Murphy.

18   Mr. President, I rise for the LEAH bill.  I 

19   wasn't that well-informed about the LEAH bill

21   my office who wanted to homeschool their 

22   children.  

23                Education is a key component to our 

24   children's lives and them being successful, and 

25   being taught at home is essential to a child's 


                                                                1906

 1   development.  There are different paths to 

 2   education -- school-based, parent-based.  

 3                But what really struck a chord in me 

 4   is that if your child is parent-based, you cannot 

 5   play sports in a public school, which to me is a 

 6   form of discrimination.  If a parent chooses to 

 7   homeschool their child and they want that child 

 8   to play sports in the school, the school should 

 9   avail themselves so these kids can be a part of 

10   playing sports.  

11                So I congratulate the sponsor of 

12   this bill.  I congratulate the parents of this 

13   bill for advocating for their children to make 

14   sure that their children can play sports, can 

15   play musical instruments, and could avail 

16   themselves to the public schools as far as 

17   extracurricular activities for their children.

18                So prior to today I wasn't sure 

19   about the LEAH bill, but seeing these young women 

20   and fathers and their children who are just so 

21   energized by being up here in Albany -- they 

22   were, you know, eager to learn, they were eager 

23   to express themselves.  And I'm saying today 

24   education is a key component for all our 

25   children.  And hopefully one day in the State of 


                                                                1907

 1   New York we will be the number-one state for 

 2   education rather than the 45th.

 3                So we have a long way to go with 

 4   education, and the parents see that our 

 5   schools are failing some of our children.  And if 

 6   our schools weren't failing some of our children, 

 7   maybe these parents wouldn't have to take matters 

 8   into their own hands.  They're saying that the 

 9   schools are failing our kids, we have to make 

10   sure our children are educated, and they're 

11   keeping them at home to educate their children.  

12                So hopefully one day we will enhance 

13   our schools so parents will feel good that their 

14   children will go to school and not be bullied, 

15   they will go to school and no one will harass 

16   them, they will not have to go to school and be 

17   exposed to drugs.  

18                So these are the things that are 

19   facing our children in schools today and why many 

20   of our schools are failing throughout the state, 

21   and these parents are saying, No, my child will 

22   be successful, my child will get a great 

23   education, I'm keeping my child at home but I do 

24   want my child to play sports, and they should be 

25   able to do so.

18                This is a piece of legislation that 

19   I've passed before in this house, and I believe 

20   that it's an important way we can close a very 

21   dangerous loophole that exists.  

22                I think most of us know that right 

23   now the law of the land in New York State bans 

24   sexual predators from living within a thousand 

25   feet of a school.  Unfortunately, now with the 


                                                                1918

 1   proliferation of UPK around the state, especially 

 2   in the City, right now they are not covered.  

 3                So in other words, a sexual 

 4   predator, under the law, can now live within a 

 5   thousand feet of a UPK program or a standalone 

 6   kindergarten.  As we know, sometimes kindergarten 

 7   programs are housed within traditional schools 

 8   that actually go from K to 8; those are covered.  

 9   But if it's a standalone kindergarten or UPK, 

10   it's not covered.

11                That's something that's extremely 

12   important.  And I think we need to close this 

13   loophole and make sure our youngest people are 

14   protected as well.

15                The next issue we find, that there 

16   really isn't an exchange between the Department 

17   of Education and the Division of Criminal Justice 

18   Services.  Especially downstate, where we see 

19   more and more schools opening up, for some reason 

20   they're not in the database of DOCCS, and they're 

21   not actually policing individuals who are living 

22   within a thousand feet of the school.  

23                I had a case in my district that a 

24   school that's three years old was not part of the 

25   law; in other words, individuals were still 


                                                                1919

 1   allowed to live near that school.  

 2                So I think a sharing of information 

 3   between the Department of Education and DOCCS is
